localBiteReport: The most current reports available for Choctawhatchee Bay are from late July/early August 2026, with the most recent individual charter post dated approximately July 27 (about 6 days ago). Speckled trout are the dominant inshore story right now — guides report trout scattered throughout the bay and still feeding actively despite windy conditions, with anglers advised to be selective about where they fish until the wind settles. Bull redfish are also in the mix and receiving a lot of attention; one recent trip landed a 40¼-inch, 26-lb bull red, and limit catches of upper-slot reds have been reported out of Santa Rosa Beach. A late-June trip on West Bay/Choctawhatchee also produced speckled trout, slot reds, and a notable 43-lb black drum, suggesting black drum remain a legitimate target around the bay system. Water temperature at this location is 85°F. Note: the Half Hitch Destin fishing report blog appears to have last posted on June 15, 2026 — no July update was findable — so that source is not reflected here.

aiSummary: Speckled trout and bull redfish are the dominant inshore story on Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with guides reporting trout scattered and feeding bay-wide and bull reds drawing serious attention — including a 40¼-inch, 26-lb fish landed recently and limit catches of upper-slot reds out of Santa Rosa Beach. Water is at 85°F and slightly stained under cloudy skies, conditions that generally favor low-light feeders and keep fish active through the morning hours. With an 88% storm chance before 4 PM today, the play is to hit exposed spots early and have a protected fallback bayou in mind before midday.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides and concentrates trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around its pilings year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on incoming tides, as fish stack up waiting for bait to sweep past. It is worth noting that the open water here is fully exposed to wind and chop — this is typically the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when conditions deteriorate.
bridge.todaysCall: High tide hits at 9:14 AM, which means the incoming current will be pushing bait through the pilings during first light — that is your best window here and it aligns perfectly with the morning low-light period before storms develop. Work the WSW lee-side pilings hard; with wind running WSW at 10–15 mph, those down-current faces will be the prime ambush zones for trout and reds. Slightly stained water actually helps here, keeping fish less wary right against the structure. However, with an 88% storm chance before 4 PM and this spot fully exposed to open-bay chop, plan to be off the bridge and running for covered water no later than 11–11:30 AM.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers some of the most reliable protected inshore fishing on this stretch of Choctawhatchee Bay, with a strong year-round redfish population and trout and flounder showing at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime structure, while tree cover keeps interior water a few degrees cooler than the open bay and provides meaningful shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish and can hold bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: With WSW winds at 10–15 mph and an 88% storm chance before 4 PM, Alaqua's tree cover and protected layout make it a smart choice for extending your fishing window safely today. Target the oyster bars at the creek mouth on the falling tide after the 9:14 AM high — moving water will concentrate bait and pull trout and reds onto the edges through late morning. Water at 85°F and slightly stained is right in the redfish comfort zone, so expect them to be feeding actively along the shallower grass and oyster structure. If storms fire early, you can push further up the creek and stay fishable while waiting for a break.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less fishing pressure than nearby Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to translate into less-educated, more aggressive fish. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, while pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It is worth noting that Basin Bayou offers less weather protection than LaGrange when conditions build.
basin.todaysCall: The falling tide after the 9:14 AM high is your window on the interior grass flats — reds will be moving off the flat edges as water drops, which combined with slightly stained water and cloudy skies keeps them less spooky than usual. Lower pressure here means fish that are quicker to commit, so if you arrive in the 9–11 AM range you should catch quality moving-water time before storm chances escalate. Keep an eye on the western sky given the WSW wind direction — storms building from that quadrant can arrive with less warning. Because Basin offers less protection than LaGrange, treat your turnaround time seriously and be heading out no later than midday.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer in this bay system, anchored by legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deeper holes inside the bayou hold black drum and sheepshead, rounding out a diverse inshore fishery. It is also the most protected water on the northern side of the bay, making it the default go-to spot when weather becomes a factor.
lagrange.todaysCall: Today LaGrange checks nearly every box: it is the most protected location on this dashboard, its oyster bars will be firing on the outgoing tide after the 9:14 AM high, and the slightly stained water under cloudy skies sets up well for both trout and reds feeding confidently in the shallows. Guides have been reporting trout scattered and actively feeding bay-wide, and LaGrange's structure-heavy interior is exactly the kind of place those fish congregate — work popping corks or soft plastics along the oyster bar edges as the tide begins to ebb. Black drum have also shown up recently in the bay system, and the deeper interior holes here are worth a few casts with cut crab or shrimp. With an 88% storm window before 4 PM, LaGrange's protected character means you can fish later into the morning with more confidence than any other spot on this dashboard.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and Choctawhatchee Bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The upper section transitions toward brackish water and holds bass alongside smaller reds, while the creek mouth is a proven flounder zone. Short and well-sheltered, it is considered the safest fishery on this side of the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: With the high tide at 9:14 AM and storms likely before 4 PM, Four Mile Creek is a smart call for anglers who want to stay protected and maximize their safe fishing window today. The creek mouth flounder zone is worth hitting as the tide transitions from high to falling, and then work up into the bends and grass edges as bait gets flushed back toward the bay on the ebb. At 85°F and slightly stained, reds in the upper bends should be actively feeding — slow presentations along grass edges and undercut banks are the move. WSW winds at 10–15 mph will barely register inside the creek, giving you a calm-water option no matter how quickly conditions deteriorate outside.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay and a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination, known for trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water during summer mornings. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides, adding a fun bonus species for anglers rigged for speed. It does see regular pressure from guides and recreational anglers, and the run from the 331 Bridge area is longer than the other bayous — factor that into your trip planning.
hogtown.todaysCall: Summer mornings are Hogtown's peak window for trout on the grass flats, and today's cloudy skies and slightly stained water extend that bite a bit later than a bluebird day would allow — target the 7–10 AM stretch before storm activity ramps up. The 9:14 AM high tide puts good water over the grass right during that prime period, ideal for working soft plastics or live shrimp under a popping cork in two to four feet. Guides have been reporting trout feeding actively and scattered throughout the bay, so Hogtown's flats should be in play. Account for the longer run time from the 331 Bridge, and absolutely be back at the dock or tucked into protected water well before noon given the 88% pre-4 PM storm window.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou, just south of Freeport, which means the oyster-bar trout and redfish patterns that make LaGrange the top producer on this dashboard plausibly extend into this quieter, smaller water. Being interior and compact, it offers calm conditions when wind builds on the open bay. There is considerably less documented fishing history for Mallet compared to LaGrange itself, so expectations should be calibrated accordingly.
mallet.todaysCall: Mallet makes the most sense today as either a quiet morning opener before committing to LaGrange or as an overflow spot if LaGrange's more popular areas have company — its direct connection to that system gives it legitimate trout and redfish potential. Work any visible oyster structure or grass edges on the falling tide after the 9:14 AM high, using the same soft-plastic or live-shrimp approach you would deploy in LaGrange. Its interior, sheltered character means WSW winds at 10–15 mph will be almost irrelevant inside, and you can tuck here safely if storms approach earlier than expected. Treat it as a calm, lower-pressure complement to LaGrange rather than a standalone headliner.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a genuine long-run destination that is not a quick local trip. It shares the protected-bayou character of Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees lighter pressure simply because of its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and can realistically be fished in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: The long run from the 331 Bridge area makes Mack Bayou a weather-dependent call today, and with an 88% storm chance before 4 PM and WSW winds at 10–15 mph, the open-bay crossing requires careful timing — leave at first light and plan your return before the late-morning storm window opens. If you make the run, the oyster bars and grass edges will be in good shape on the falling tide after the 9:14 AM high, and slightly stained water under cloud cover keeps trout and reds in a feeding mood throughout the morning. Light pressure means fish that are less conditioned to boat traffic and more willing to bite. Pair it with a quick stop at Hewett on the way back, but build a hard turnaround time into your plan given today's storm risk.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, sharing the same protected-bayou habitat of oyster bars, marsh grass at the mouth, and deeper interior holes further in. Like its neighbor, it benefits from light pressure due to its distance from the primary boat ramps. It pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou and is best treated as part of a dedicated south-shore run rather than a standalone trip.
hewett.todaysCall: The same long-run caution that applies to Mack Bayou applies here — with an 88% storm chance before 4 PM, committing to the barrier-island side requires an early departure and a firm turnaround time well before midday. If the run is on, work Hewett's mouth structure on the falling tide after the 9:14 AM high, then probe any deeper interior holes for trout and reds in the slightly stained, 85°F water. Cloudy skies and stained conditions should keep fish less wary and feeding longer than they would on a calm, clear summer day. Treat Hewett as the middle stop between Mack and Buck Bayou on the same south-shore trip, not a standalone destination.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should broadly track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis for confident specific claims about fish behavior or holding areas here. It is best approached as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a primary destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou only makes sense today as a brief add-on if you are already making the long south-shore run to Mack and Hewett — do not treat the extra distance and time as worthwhile on a day with an 88% storm chance before 4 PM. If you do swing through, fish it the same way you would its neighbors: oyster edges and grass structure on the falling tide after the 9:14 AM high, with soft plastics or shrimp for trout and reds in the slightly stained water. Keep your time here short and prioritize getting back across open water before storm activity develops. On a calmer, lower-risk day, it could be a productive bonus stop on the same trip.
